bio.en: Laura Modi is the co-founder and CEO of Bobbie, an organic infant-formula brand, and previously spent years at Airbnb leading hospitality and host community efforts.
bio.zh: 劳拉·莫迪（Laura Modi）是有机婴儿配方奶粉品牌 Bobbie 的联合创始人兼 CEO，此前在 Airbnb 工作多年，负责款待体验与房东社群。

summary.en: Laura shares how Bobbie's head of growth flagged that they were depleting inventory faster than they could replenish, and made the tough call to pause growth to protect existing customers. She explains the discipline of defending your core promise even when demand is skyrocketing. The episode is a lesson in values-driven scaling and saying no at the right moment.
summary.zh: 劳拉讲述了 Bobbie 的增长负责人如何发现库存消耗快于补货速度，并做出暂停增长以保护现有用户的艰难决定。她阐释了即便需求暴涨，也要守住核心承诺的纪律。本期是一堂关于"以价值观驱动扩张、在正确的时刻说不"的课。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: So our head of growth, who... I mean, this girl is just fabulous. She was watching our inventory levels very carefully and also watching how quickly we were growing. And I'll never forget that moment. I can visualize it, sitting in a meeting, and she pulls up her screen. She goes, "Here's the dilemma. We are depleting inventory far quicker than our ability to replenish and the customers keep coming." You sit there and your first reaction is "This is great. We're growing." And she's like, "It's not that great, actually, because here's what's going to happen. We are going to run out of product for the babies that are on Bobbie today. We have about six days before we get to a place where we won't be able to serve those who've already made a commitment to Bobbie." She's like, "So we need to turn off our site and stop growing the business."
turns.zh: 于是，我们的增长部门负责人……说真的，这个女孩真是太棒了。她一直密切关注着我们的库存水平，也密切关注着我们的增长速度。我永远都忘不了那一刻。我能想象当时的情景——在开会时，她打开屏幕说：“现在有个难题。我们消耗库存的速度远远超过了补货的速度，而客户的需求却源源不断。” 你坐在那里，第一反应是“这太棒了，说明我们业务在增长。” 但她却说：“其实这并不好，因为接下来会发生这样的情况——我们现有的库存很快就会被用完，无法继续为已经在Bobbie平台上下单的客户提供服务。” 她接着说：“所以我们现在必须关闭网站，停止业务扩张。”

turns.en: Highly approved.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.en: We'll see. We'll see how it ends up. It'll be a good retrospective.
turns.zh: 走着瞧吧。看看最后结果如何。应该会是一次不错的回顾。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Merlot's so good.
turns.zh: 梅洛酒真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I thought it'd be fun to start with just your time at Airbnb where we got to work together. You spent five and a half years there. Everyone that spends that amount of time at Airbnb, and let me know if you agree, always ends up being in this transformative time in their life and their career. Yeah, okay, you're nodding.
turns.zh: 我想先从你在Airbnb的工作经历说起，我们曾共事过五年半。每个在Airbnb待这么久的人（如果你认同的话），总会经历人生和事业中一个蜕变的时期。嗯，好的，你点头了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I can't imagine a world where I would be without Airbnb.
turns.zh: 我无法想象如果没有Airbnb，我的世界会是怎样的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I feel the same way. And so I want to spend a little time on what you learned from that experience and what you took away there. But just to start, can you just share briefly what you worked on while you were at Airbnb?
turns.zh: 是啊，我也这么觉得。所以我想花点时间聊聊你从那段经历中学到了什么，又收获了什么。但首先，你能简单分享一下你在Airbnb工作期间负责的项目吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, what didn't we work on? Just, I reflect back and it's one of those experiences where it probably was transformative because you do get an opportunity to work on so many different things. So I remember joining and I was just put in charge of leading and growing parts of customer service, vendor management. I mean, we were scaling the team so fast on that side. It quickly shifted into taking me to Europe where I led our consolidation of our European offices in Dublin. It was so funny. I remember at the time being asked to go do it and thinking, am I being asked purely because I'm just the only Irish person in the company right now? But it was one of the biggest operational changes that we went through there. And then for the last few years I was the director of hospitality leading global host community and host operations.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们没做过什么？回想起来，这段经历可能具有变革性意义，因为你确实有机会参与众多不同领域的工作。我记得刚加入公司时，就被委以重任，负责领导和发展客户服务及供应商管理团队。当时我们在这些部门扩张得非常快。很快我就被派往欧洲，负责整合都柏林的欧洲办事处。这事儿挺有趣的。我记得当时被要求去那里工作，心里还在想，他们是不是因为我是公司里唯一的爱尔兰人而选我？但那确实是我们经历过的最大规模的运营变革之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you're underselling that last part. Can you just share a little bit more of what that actually means?
turns.zh: 我觉得你低估了最后那部分的意义了。能再多分享一下这具体意味着什么吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Our product really wasn't our technology. It wasn't the technology that we were building, although for a few years we all thought it was. And then it got to a place where we realized Airbnb is nothing without its hosts, nothing. If anything, Airbnb's product was its hosts. So there was a moment, and I can't remember, it was two or three years in, where that narrative was building up more and more and we realized that there was a need to have a central team, which we called Hospitality, dedicated to equipping and recognizing and holding this product of our hosts accountable to their job.
turns.zh: 我们的产品其实不是技术本身。虽然有几年时间我们都以为是技术，但后来我们意识到，没有房东，Airbnb就什么都不是。可以说，Airbnb的产品就是房东。所以有一刻，我记不清是两三年后的事了，这种观念逐渐深入人心，我们意识到需要成立一个专门的团队——我们称之为"房东团队"——致力于赋能、表彰房东，并监督他们履行职责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think we could go down that. Maybe let me ask one question there because I think that's really interesting. For a company where the product, as you said, and marketplaces in general, the product you're selling is the supply, in our case Airbnb hosts. Is there something maybe you learned from that experience, I don't know, working at a software, company about how to think about the supply as the product and how that maybe informs, I don't know, what you're building today or just something in general?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得我们可以深入探讨一下。或许让我先问个问题，我觉得这很有意思。对于一家像Airbnb这样的公司，产品（如你所说）以及一般的市场平台，其核心产品就是供应商——在我们这里，就是Airbnb的房东。那么，你是否从这段经历中学到了一些东西，比如在软件公司工作，如何将供应商视为产品，以及这如何影响你现在的工作或整体思路？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I think it maybe just starts internally where you have to be able to create a culture first, to all understand that. Because otherwise you're going to be in a position where you're focused on optimizing the technology, efficiency, growth, looking at tools for tools' sake versus tools for users' sake. And I mean, I remember a very pivotal shift when we started realizing that we really needed to understand our hosts far more than we had leading up to that. And I think growth just follows. I mean, we certainly saw that at Airbnb. If we put the hosts first and we thought about building tools for them versus what do we need just to drive more bookings, users begets users, and that's exactly what we saw.
turns.zh: 我认为这或许始于内部——你必须先营造一种文化，让所有人都理解这一点。否则，你就会陷入专注于优化技术、效率和增长，仅为了工具而使用工具，而非为了用户利益而开发工具的境地。我记得当我们意识到需要比此前更深入地了解房东时，那是一个至关重要的转变。我认为增长自然会随之而来——我们在Airbnb就见证了这一点。若我们以房东为先，致力于为他们开发工具，而非只为获取更多预订量而优化平台，用户自然会带来更多用户，这正是我们所见证的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some lasting lessons from your time at Airbnb that you bring to what you're working on now?
turns.zh: 在Airbnb的经历中，你获得了哪些持久的启示，正在应用于当前的工作中？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: The most obvious kind of cliched one is culture. It is bread and butter to everything you do, from the people you hire to how you build the right mindset to just keeping the energy. I mean, energy at Airbnb was the currency. It was like, unless you didn't have that energy, nothing was happening. And I think about that every day. How do you keep energy going? And my God, they did that for a decade, just keeping it going. I think the other big takeaway is if you can get people excited behind a vision and storytelling, it again kind of carries through that cross-functional work. (00:09:16): I now reflect back on just how powerful our storytelling was at Airbnb to get people pumped up. I mean, even for some of the smallest features that we would build, Lenny, they would kick off with the most powerful storytelling. I mean, we were changing lives. And again, it makes you wake up every day going, "Fuck, yeah, I want to work on this." And you're not just going in to fix something, you actually feel like you're having very large impact. And that has to be felt the whole way down the org.
turns.zh: 最显而易见的教训当属文化。它是你所做一切的核心，从招聘人才、建立正确的思维模式，到维持团队活力。在Airbnb，活力就是通行货币。若缺乏这种能量，任何事情都无法推进。我每天都在思考如何保持这种活力。天哪，他们坚持了十年才做到这一点。我认为另一个重要启示是，若能让人们为愿景和故事所激动，这种激情就能贯穿跨职能协作。（00:09:16）：回首在Airbnb的岁月，我们的故事讲述能力之强令人惊叹。即便开发一些最微小的功能，Lenny也会以最震撼的故事开场。我们在改变人们的生活。这让你每天醒来时都会想：“去他的，我要做这件事。”你不只是去修复问题，而是真切感受到自己在产生重大影响，这种感觉必须在整个组织中深入人心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you're already getting into the specifics of what culture actually... how it manifests and how to build a culture. And so I want to maybe ask another question there. You talked about keeping the energy up is a big part of creating the culture. You want to create strong storytelling, either in one of those buckets or another example. What do you do at Bobbie, which we're going to talk about, to build a strong culture? What else do you do to actually do that? Because people hear about building a strong culture and they're like, "What do I do? How do I do that?" So I'd love to hear anything you've actually done there.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你已经深入探讨了文化的具体内涵——它的表现形式以及如何构建文化。因此我想再追问一句。你提到保持活力是文化建设的重要组成部分。你希望通过强有力的故事讲述来凝聚团队，或者举其他例子。在Bobbie（我们稍后会谈及），你们采取了哪些措施来构建强大的文化？还做了哪些具体工作？因为人们一听说要构建强大文化，往往会问：“该怎么做？从何入手？”所以我很想听听你们的实际经验。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I think one of the biggest ones I would say is that you need to get to know people personally as much as you do professionally. And that was maybe something I also maybe took a little bit for granted at Airbnb. We had built a culture where people really personally loved each other. They loved working together. Now, fast-forward to today and you're building a company that's completely remote, how do you build a personal relationship? (00:10:36): For example, we make sure that we take time to have personal and professional check-ins. And cross-functional people in the org who maybe have no idea someone else as a kid or what they're doing in their lives. Because those personal connections, I mean, again, it's your second family, you're waking up every day to spend time with them. I think those personal connections are some of the biggest.
turns.zh:
我认为其中最重要的一点是，你需要像在职场中那样去了解同事的个人生活。或许这也是我在Airbnb时曾忽视的一点——我们曾营造出一种文化，让同事们真心喜欢彼此，享受共事的时光。如今，面对完全远程办公的公司，如何建立起这种个人联系呢？（00:10:36）  
比如，我们会确保定期进行个人和工作层面的沟通。组织中的跨职能成员或许并不了解彼此的童年经历或生活近况。这些个人联系意义非凡——毕竟同事们就是你的第二个家庭，每天醒来都能与他们共度时光。这种真挚的情感连接无疑是成功的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting because there's also this movement away from your workmates or your family. Airbnb I think is very... Everyone called themselves AirFam, but that becomes challenging when you have to let people go and there's challenging times. So is your perspective, that's where you find value, to kind of stay close to that?
turns.zh: 这很有意思，因为人们总在远离工作伙伴或家庭。Airbnb曾号称"Air家人，"但当不得不裁员或面临挑战时，这种亲密感就会土崩瓦解。您认为保持这种亲密感是关键吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I think you need a hybrid. I do. I think looking at work for transactions' sake, are your colleagues purely as the people who are just there to get the job done with you? That's not inspiring. No. Do I think that there's a balance and maybe some of the things that get introduced in a culture probably don't need to go that far? Yeah. But no matter what, I do believe building personal connections and actually caring about the people you work for is imperative for building a lasting business.
turns.zh: 我认为需要找到平衡。我认为若仅将工作视为交易，那么同事就只是完成任务的伙伴。这毫无激励作用。不，我认为应当找到平衡，或许有些文化导入的举措本不必走得太远？没错。但无论如何，建立个人联系、真正关心共事伙伴，对打造可持续的企业至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the story of going from Airbnb to building a baby formula?
turns.zh: 从Airbnb转行到婴儿配方奶粉行业，背后有什么故事？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my god. You mean leaving one of the fastest growing companies to start powdered milk? It was so funny. I don't know if I ever shared this with you, Lenny. I remember telling my dad and he was like, "Hold on a second, Laura. I don't understand." He's like, "You're lactose intolerant. Why are you starting a milk company?" He just couldn't fathom why I would, I mean in many ways, leave an established business that had established parental leave benefits, everything that in many ways, as you grow through your career, become more and more what you need and you need the stability. (00:12:30): So that shift, I suppose, just socializing it is probably one of the hardest. And it's a big thing to take a risk because you're taking 10 steps backwards in hopes of making major leaps forward. And I think that's just always kind of been a narrative mostly in my career, which is I don't believe there's such a thing as taking a big leap without first taking a major risk, and that was. I mean, it was a very big risk, obviously. But then also, keep in mind, even before I joined Airbnb, I had a good job at Google. And Airbnb at the time, I think, just had one of its most major crises back in 2011.
turns.zh: 天哪。你是说要离开一家发展最快的公司去创办奶粉公司？太搞笑了。我不知道我有没有跟你提过这事，莱尼。我记得我跟我爸说的时候，他一脸困惑：“等等，劳拉，我不明白。”他说：“你乳糖不耐受啊，为什么要创办一家奶粉公司？”他根本无法理解我为什么要离开一家已经建立完善的产假福利体系、各方面都成熟且符合职业发展需求的公司。（00:12:30）所以这种转变，或许最难的就是让别人理解。冒险一试总是件大事，因为你要先退后十步，才能向前大踏步。我觉得这在我职业生涯中一直是个主旋律——我不相信不先冒险就能实现飞跃，而这次确实是个很大的冒险。当然，加入爱彼家之前，我在谷歌的工作也很不错。但当时的爱彼家正经历2011年的重大危机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: CJ or EJ?
turns.zh: CJ还是EJ？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: EJ. EJ incident. It was all over the papers. It was a small company. I wasn't really given a title. And I'll never forget as well, exactly the same narrative. My parents going, "Hold on a second. You're leaving Google to go start a B&B." Like, "No, I'm not starting a B&B. I really believe this company's going somewhere." So anyway, the moral of the story is the move into starting my own business, it was a big risk and it was one that I felt so confident on that was needed, it was worth it.
turns.zh: EJ。EJ事件。当时铺天盖地都是新闻。那是个小公司，我甚至没有正式头衔。我永远忘不了父母的反应：“等等，你要离开谷歌去开民宿？”我说：“不，我不是开民宿。我真的相信这家公司有前途。”总之，这个故事的启示是，投身创业是一次重大冒险，但我对自己的选择充满信心，认为这是必要的，也是值得的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some people do what you did there, where you take a big risk and kind of maybe stick backwards and it doesn't work out. And in your case it's worked out many times. Is there a thread across the decisions you've made that you think people maybe should look for or you think is important in taking that big risk? Or do you think it was a lot of super luck?
turns.zh: 有些人会像你那样冒险，可能会退步但最终失败。而你多次成功了。在你做过的这些决定中，有没有一条主线值得人们借鉴，或者你认为对冒险至关重要？还是说这只是运气好？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Super luck. I mean, I have a folder of businesses and product ideas that, prior to Bobbie, I had dreamt of. And we can always get into that again in the future. Some of them I still dream of doing one day, but a big reason for not taking the risk is because I didn't feel the conviction. So, yes, while I think it's luck, I think I put a lot of intention into researching the marketplace, understanding the business, determining how much of a risk I'm really able to take, even financially. Sitting with my husband and determining how long I may need to be in this position before raising capital and is it possible? It certainly isn't what sometimes it can appear on the surface, which is, "Oh, she had an idea and she left." There's a lot of work that goes into determining is this actually going to be something that's viable?
turns.zh: 真是太幸运了。我的意思是，在认识博比之前，我就有过一个文件夹，里面存储着各种商业创意和产品构想。未来我们或许还会再聊起这些构想。其中有些项目我至今仍渴望有朝一日付诸实践，但之所以迟迟未能冒险尝试，主要是因为我缺乏坚定的信念。所以，虽然我觉得这确实是运气使然，但我也确实投入了大量精力去研究市场、了解业务、评估自己能承受多大的风险——甚至包括财务方面的风险。与丈夫一起探讨这个问题时，我们会仔细分析：在筹集资金之前，我可能需要在这个位置上坚守多久？这是否可行？现实往往与表面现象大相径庭——人们往往会想：“哦，她只是灵光一现，随便选了Airbnb就成功了。” 但你所讲述的历程表明，成功绝非偶然——它需要投入大量心血去验证一个项目是否切实可行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that lesson. It may seem like Laura went to here, to Airbnb and was just like, "Oh, how lucky she picked Airbnb of all the companies." But what you're saying is you spent the time researching, seeing what the company started.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你的这番见解。表面看来，劳拉似乎是随意选了Airbnb，运气爆棚。但你提到她花了大量时间研究市场，观察这家公司的起步阶段。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So let's talk about Bobbie, just broadly. Can you just talk about what is Bobbie and then what is the scale of Bobbie these days? What stats can you share to give people a sense of how large this has gotten?
turns.zh: 是的。好的，那我们先大致聊聊Bobbie吧。能先讲讲Bobbie是什么吗？再说说它目前的规模有多大？能分享一些数据，让大家感受一下它已经发展到了什么程度？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Bobbie is a powdered milk company. We are an infant formula. And prior to infant formula, the formula-gate of 2022, which everyone is now familiar with. The short of it is that this is an industry that is owned by a duopoly. It's one of the last remaining industries in the CPG space that has seen any disruption or change in probably 40 years. And my desire was to create a formula that parents could feel proud of, an infant formula that felt modern and met where science is today. Because frankly, none of the infant formulas on the market really had caught up to where science has evolved to. (00:16:00): Now, obviously, I only experienced this as becoming a mother myself. I knew nothing about this at all. And then I pick up a can of formula and I read the back of the can and there's ingredients in there I would never feed myself. And I think the thing that really hit me, and this was more of the business investor side of me, I just hated the product and I couldn't understand why, as something that is used by so many, 83% of parents, why is it that I'm embarrassed about it? I feel guilty feeding my child this and it's also ugly. It's sitting on my counter every day and this isn't what I want to see. (00:16:41): I remember saying to my husband, "I feel like we have failed to breastfeed." And the alternative is that I need to give her a medical solution to survive, which it's milk. I should feel like I'm giving her food. But for whatever reason, society has set this up to make formula feel like you have failed. I mean, that was the impetus. I know you asked me, what is Bobbie? We are a better-for-you infant formula without the guilt.
turns.zh: Bobbie是一家婴儿配方奶粉公司。我们专注于婴儿配方奶粉。说到婴儿配方奶粉，就不得不提2022年那场震惊全行业的“配方奶粉门”事件，大家应该都听说过。简而言之，这个行业由两家巨头把持，几乎是消费品领域中40年来唯一没有经历重大变革的行业。我的初衷是打造一款让父母引以为傲的配方奶粉，一款既符合现代科技标准又贴合科学研究成果的婴儿配方奶粉。因为说实话，市面上的婴儿配方奶粉几乎都跟不上科学研究的步伐。（00:16:00）当然，我自己成为母亲后才真正体会到这些。我之前对这个行业一无所知。当时拿起一罐配方奶粉，看看背面的成分表，里面有些成分我自己都舍不得给孩子吃。这件事真正触动我的，更多是从商业投资者的角度出发——我实在不喜欢市面上的产品，实在不明白为什么会有83%的父母选择用这种产品，却还要为此感到羞耻？我觉得给孩子喂这种奶粉简直是在犯罪。它每天摆在厨房台面上，我实在不愿看到这样的场景。（00:16:41）我记得当时对丈夫说：“我感觉我们母乳喂养失败了。”而唯一的选择就是用奶粉来维持孩子的生命，这本该是喂养孩子的食物。但不知为何，社会却把配方奶粉描绘成一种失败的象征。这就是我的初衷。我知道你问我Bobbie是什么？我们是一款让父母无负担的婴儿配方奶粉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ooh, I like that. That was a good summary at the end. How about about the scale of Bobbie? What kind of numbers can you share? Just to give people a sense of how large this has become.
turns.zh: 哦，我喜欢你最后的总结。关于Bobbie的规模呢？能分享一下数据吗？让大家感受一下它已经发展到了什么程度。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah. Oh, my god. I remember launching, it was 100% direct-to-consumer, it was at the top of 2021. And the moment you're about to launch, the first question all investors ask is what do you believe your growth is going to be? First question. It's the same question you get after you're married, when are you going to have a baby? I'm like, "I have no clue what my growth is going to be. I've been on the market for a hot minute." I remember thinking hopefully four million, five million in our first year. So the growth has been fabulous and beyond our wildest dreams in what we had expected.
turns.zh: 是啊。天哪。我记得我们刚推出产品时，完全是直销模式，2021年初。刚要上线时，所有投资者问的第一个问题就是：你预计增长率会达到多少？这就是婚后人们问你的第一个问题——什么时候生孩子？我当时回答：“我根本不知道增长率会怎样，我才刚进入市场没多久。”我记得当时希望第一年能做到四五百万的销售额。结果增长速度远超预期，甚至超出了我们最疯狂的想象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. There's a bunch of questions I'm going to ask about how you grew Bobby, but you mentioned the COVID baby shortage crisis. And there's a couple stories I wanted to get into that was one of them. Can you just talk about what you went through in that period? Because I imagine it was both a blessing and a curse. Also, it reminds me, I have a friend who uses Bobbie and she just told me a story about how someone, she couldn't find any Bobbie during COVID, supply chain issues and all that, and an employee of Bobbie came to her house and brought her formula just to make sure she had enough. And obviously that created forever brand loyalty. And we'll talk a little bit about brand, but I'd love to hear about just that period of the journey and what you learned from it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我有好多问题想问你关于如何把Bobby发展壮大的，但你提到了新冠疫情期间婴儿配方奶粉短缺的危机。这正是我想深入探讨的案例之一。你能否谈谈那段时期的经历？想必那既是机遇也是挑战。说到这儿，我突然想起有个朋友也在用Bobby。她刚跟我讲过一个故事：新冠期间因为供应链问题，找不到Bobby产品。结果Bobby的一位员工直接上门送货，确保她能有充足的配方奶粉供应。这显然为品牌赢得了永久的忠诚度。我们稍后会深入探讨品牌策略，但我更想听听你如何度过那段艰难时期，以及从中汲取了哪些经验教训。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: There is nothing like a crisis that gives you more of an appreciation for what opportunity lies ahead. And I would thank my blessings every day that the only way to look at this positively was to be in a position of gratitude that I have an opportunity that most startups would wait a lifetime for. So what happened was I woke up one day and the President of the United States was talking about there being an infant formula shortage. And again, it's just being in the right place at the right time. A topic that never has really been brought up. Unfortunately, one of the large companies, one of the duopolies, had a recall and that recall basically left the nation without product and we were not able to feed babies in the US. (00:19:29): Being one of the smallest companies here, we ended up seeing our customer count double the first week that that shortage happened. All of that would seem great, almost like a dream for any startup to be in, that you're going to see your product grow now because they're moving from one customer to another or from one product to another. But here's what happens. Infant formula is one of those products you can't run out of. It's not cool to be out of infant formula. It's not like a piece of furniture and you're at capacity for a certain amount of time. (00:20:03): So our Head of Growth who, I mean this girl is just fabulous. She was watching our inventory levels very carefully and also watching how quickly we were growing. And I'll never forget that moment. I can visualize it, sitting in a meeting. And she pulls up her screen, she goes, "Here's the dilemma. We are depleting inventory far quicker than our ability to replenish. And the customers keep coming." You sit there and your first reaction is, "I mean, this is great. We're growing." And she's like, "It's not that great, actually, because here's what's going to happen. We are going to run out a product for the babies that are on Bobbie today. That's a problem." (00:20:48): So in my absorption of everything that's happening, and again, being a company that had only been on the market 14 months, saying to her, "Well, Shireen, what do we do next?" And she's like, "We have about six days before we get to a place where we won't be able to serve those who've already made a commitment to Bobbie." She's like, "So we need to turn off our site and stop growing the business." That's a big decision to make when you're like, "Okay, so I'm going to turn to all of our investors and say we're turning off our site, we're closing down to ensure that we keep enough product." (00:21:23): But honestly, in hindsight, it was a no-brainer. We were not going to run out of product on our current subscribers and we had no idea how long the crisis was going to last. So even though we didn't know how long we'd be off, I gave the thumbs up, sally forth, turn it off, and we went into hibernation mode. And in many ways we switched immediately into our customers come first. We now have 70,000 subscribers who are in a place of panic because they hear the news every day that there's formula running out and our job is to give them confidence and clarity that we have the products for them and we're never going to run out. And we did. For six months, six months, we kept our website off and we didn't grow the business last year and we continued to serve our current subscribers and in the end we became the only formula company that was able to reliably serve its current customers and never run out.
turns.zh:
没有什么比危机更能让你深刻意识到未来机遇的珍贵。我每天都心怀感恩，因为唯有怀着感恩之心看待此事——我才意识到，多数初创公司梦寐以求的机会，我如今却已轻易获得。事情是这样的，有一天我醒来时，美国总统正在谈论婴儿配方奶粉短缺的问题。说来也巧，这正是天时地利的巧合。这个话题从未被广泛提及。不幸的是，一家大型企业——一家双头垄断巨头——因产品召回事件，导致全美市场断货，美国婴儿无法正常喂养。（00:19:29）作为一家规模最小的公司，我们在配方奶粉短缺的第一周就迎来了客户数量翻倍的惊喜。表面看，这一切堪称完美，仿佛初创企业的梦想成真——产品需求激增，客户从零到一，市场从单一产品拓展。但现实远非想象中美好。

婴儿配方奶粉属于不可缺少的必需品。断货绝非易事，不像家具产品那样可临时补充库存。（00:20:03）我们的增长主管——这个女孩太出色了——时刻关注库存水平和业务增长速度。我至今难忘那次会议场景。她打开屏幕说：“问题来了——库存消耗速度远超补货速度，而客户需求还在增长。”我第一反应是：“这太棒了，说明我们发展迅速。”她却冷静回应：“其实这很危险。现有用户的配方奶粉库存将告罄，这才是大问题。”（00:20:48）面对危机，初创仅14个月的我们不得不迅速决策。我问：“希琳，我们该怎么办？”她说：“六天内必须关闭网站，停止扩张。” 当我不得不向投资者宣布停服通知时，这无疑是艰难抉择。但事后看来，此举无需犹豫。既能保证现有用户供应，又无需预测危机持续时间。即便不知道停服时长，我还是果断决策：关闭网站，进入休眠模式。转眼间，我们将客户利益置于首位，如今用户已达7万。
订阅用户们陷入了恐慌，因为他们每天都会听到奶粉即将告罄的消息。我们的职责是让他们安心并明确告知，我们有充足的产品储备，绝不会出现断货的情况。事实也的确如此。过去六个月里，我们一直关闭官网，去年业务未能扩展，但始终坚持为现有订阅用户提供服务，最终成为唯一一家能够持续为现有客户供货且从未出现断货的奶粉企业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing story. I haven't heard that before. You threw out this term at some point when we were emailing earlier of slowth, you called it a slowth. Slow growth, I think.
turns.zh: 真是个令人惊叹的故事。我之前从未听过这个故事。之前我们聊天时，你曾用“slowth”这个词来形容经济增长缓慢，我记得你当时说的是“slowth”。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my gosh.
turns.zh: 哦，我的天！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that how you think about this?
turns.zh: 你就是这么看待这件事的吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: That was part of also how do you change the culture internally? I had 60 people on the team who were all in a position of driving growth and many of them were probably only hired weeks before the shortage with the position of growth, email growth, paid acquisition. And all of a sudden you're telling someone who just left a cushy job to join a startup that we're no longer growing. And in fact, your job now is to completely flip what you thought you were going to do on its head. So we named the entire growth team, the slowth team.
turns.zh: 这也是关于如何从内部改变企业文化的部分挑战。当时我们团队有60人，每个人都肩负着推动业务增长的重任，其中许多人是在增长部门人手不足、邮件增长放缓、付费获客陷入困境的几周前才被紧急招募的。突然间，你要告诉那些刚刚辞去安稳工作加入初创公司的人——我们现在不再增长了。事实上，你现在的任务是彻底推翻原有的工作思路。因此，我们把整个增长团队命名为“慢牛团队”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: And I mean, they got creative. At some point we were emailing subscribers to nudge them to cancel because we were looking for a way to ensure that we could keep product, and my God, it was a mind-boggling moment.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，他们发挥了创造力。有段时间，我们甚至给订阅用户发邮件，催促他们取消订阅，因为我们正在寻找确保产品库存的方法。天哪，那真是令人震惊的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What else did you learn from that period that has either stuck with you in this time and/or is there something maybe you think you would've done differently if you could go back?
turns.zh: 从那段经历中，你还学到了什么？哪些经验至今对你仍有启发？或者说，如果你能回到过去，是否会有不同的做法？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Well, I have a personal belief of never looking back and regretting or changing things, but there were definitely some learnings and I would say on the positive end, some of the biggest learnings were just the power of storytelling and bringing the impact of what we were doing back into the company. I'm in a fortunate position as the CEO where, whether I'm speaking to advisors or on panels or engaging the outside world a lot more, I was able to truly feel, I mean, viscerally feel the impact that we were having by doing this. (00:24:13): I'll never forget, I was speaking at Davos on this topic and I had a customer. Oh my God, Lenny, this moment. I was standing outside of this events area and this woman comes running up to me and she's bawling, crying, and this is at a global leader's conference and she's crying and she just held my hands. And she's like, "Oh my God, you saved my life over the last year." She's like, "You have no idea the impact that Bobbie played in our lives by making the decision and giving me confidence that you weren't going to run out of product on us." (00:24:53): And that emotional connection of just, wow, yes, we may have grown the business faster, we may have gotten product back, but at the end of the day, these 70,000 voices that are out there and the stories that they have and bringing those back to the company, it's undeniable the impact, by making that decision, we've had. And I think the rest of the company feels it, too.
turns.zh: 嗯，我个人坚信永远不回头后悔或改变过去，但确实有一些收获。从积极的角度来说，最大的收获之一就是讲故事的力量，以及将我们所做工作的影响反馈到公司内部。作为CEO，我很幸运，无论是与顾问交流、参加小组讨论，还是更多地与外界互动，我都能真切地感受到——我是指发自内心的感受到——我们所做工作的影响力。（00:24:13）我永远不会忘记，我在达沃斯论坛上就这个话题发言时，遇到了一位客户。天哪，伦尼，那一刻。我站在活动区外，一位女士跑过来抱着我哭。她在全球领袖会议上哭泣，紧紧抓住我的手。她说：“天哪，过去一年你救了我的命。”她说：“你根本不知道博比的决定对我们生活的影响，让我相信产品不会断货。”（00:24:53）这种情感共鸣令人震惊。是的，我们或许让业务增长更快，拿回了产品库存，但归根结底，全球7万名用户的声音，以及他们背后的故事，再次传递到公司内部，这种影响力是不可否认的。我相信公司的其他人也能感受到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This connects with something we've brought up a couple of times now, which is just brand and brand building. Clearly, it's something that you've spent a lot of energy on and something you've done incredibly well. I think every mom I know knows of Bobbie. By the way, let me just throw this out there. I don't know if I've told you this, but I'm having a kid and we're going to get some Bobbie.
turns.zh: 这和我们之前多次提到的品牌及品牌建设息息相关。显然，你在这方面投入了大量精力，而且做得非常出色。我认识的每个妈妈都知道Bobbie这个品牌。顺便说一句，我要透露个消息，不知道有没有跟你说过，我马上要迎来宝宝了，我们打算给宝宝买些Bobbie的产品。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: What?
turns.zh: 什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh my god, Lenny's going to be a dad. This is so exciting.
turns.zh: 天哪，伦尼要当爸爸了。这真是太令人兴奋了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, this is going to be a whole new direction.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪，这又将开启全新的生活篇章了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I've got your milk, if you need it, of course, if Michelle's in a position and she wants it, we're here for you.
turns.zh: 我这儿有你的母乳，要是你需要的话。当然，如果米歇尔方便且愿意用，我们随时为你服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I appreciate that. We're going to get a deal.
turns.zh: 好的，我很感激。咱们会达成协议的。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my God, I'm so excited for you.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪，我真为你高兴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you. Laura, I feel like we need some formula just in case, right? Doesn't that-
turns.zh: 谢谢。劳拉，我觉得咱们还是备些配方奶粉以防万一，对吧？这样做不是——

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: You do. You do. And the rule is you have to try it, as well.
turns.zh: 确实要备着。而且规定是，你也得先试试看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, okay.
turns.zh: 哦，好的呀。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah. If baby's going to try it, you need to give it a shot.
turns.zh: 是啊。要是宝宝要尝试，你就得先试试看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay, okay. Oh, I'll get ready for that. I like that rule. I like that rule. Okay. There's so many things to get used to.
turns.zh: 好的。好的，好的。哦，我会准备好的。我喜欢这条规定。我喜欢这条规定。好的。要适应的东西太多了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: We'll talk again.
turns.zh: 回头再聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so going back to my question about brand, basically I just want to understand what have you learned about building a brand and when do you think it is important to invest there?
turns.zh: 好的，回到我关于品牌建设的问题。基本上，我想了解一下你在品牌建设方面有什么心得，以及你认为什么时候投资品牌建设比较重要？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, it all depends on what your product is, but the first thing I've learned about it is you have to build a brand that connects with what your customers are going through, and the experience. I once had someone say to me, "Think about who your customer is and that one customer, the exact person, is going to wake up tomorrow morning and there's going to be three things that are just playing on them in the back of their mind, the things that keep them up at night. And if you are not solving for one of those, then you're going to be finding a way to build a brand and to get in the way of that, get in the way of their mindset, have them remember who you are or what you're about." (00:27:06): And it was very clear to us that everything, from who our brand was, what it stood for, the positioning, needed to be something that parents were really finding as a struggle in that first year in feeding. So you see it in our messaging, you see it in our creative. I have no desire to bombard people with something that isn't part of those top three things that they're experiencing. Otherwise, we will have companies out there and brands out there being loud for no reason. And I think that's continued to help us in every time we have to reframe or relaunch something, to keep remembering what do they care about, let's build a brand for them.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，这一切都取决于你的产品是什么，但我学到的首要经验是，你必须打造一个能与客户经历和情感共鸣的品牌。我曾听有人对我说："想想你的客户是谁——那个具体的客户，明天早上醒来时，他们的脑海中会有三件事挥之不去，那些让他们夜不能寐的烦恼。如果你没有解决其中之一，那么你就得想办法建立品牌，切入他们的思维模式，让他们记住你是谁，你的主张是什么。"（00:27:06）  
我们很清楚，从品牌定位、品牌主张到产品定位，都必须与父母在婴儿喂养第一年的痛点紧密相连。这体现在我们的营销信息和创意设计中。我不想用那些与前三位痛点无关的内容去轰炸用户，否则我们就会看到很多品牌为了出风头而大肆宣传。但每次我们需要重新定位或重塑品牌时，牢记客户的核心需求始终是最重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that. That is such a good reminder of just, you are not going to convince someone they have a problem unless you're just spending endless money hammering into their head there's a new problem you have. If you connect to something they already know is a problem and just make it clear this is a solution to a problem, life gets a lot easier.
turns.zh: 这观点真不错。这让我深刻意识到，除非你不计代价地反复强调新问题，否则很难让别人相信自己有问题。若能触及他们已知的痛点，并清晰传达解决方案，事半功倍。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Although I know that you also have to kind of fight this breastfeeding-is-best kind of thing. So in a sense you also have to convince people this isn't what you think it is.
turns.zh: 不过我知道，在母乳喂养这件事上，你们还得应对"母乳喂养最优"的观念。所以在某种程度上，你们还得说服人们，母乳喂养并非唯一的选择。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah. And then, what's the saying? If you're explaining, you're losing. And I think there's a part of this where there's going to be a large group of people that are always going to be in the mindset that breast is the only way to do it, and anyone who does otherwise is doing second best. And I'm not there to try and convince them. I think a part of this is amplifying those that are in need of our products, that are the 83% using formula and make sure that they feel heard. But that has been a learning. I mean, that's been a huge brand learning. How do you not lean into or amplify the voices that shouldn't be heard and in many ways just get distracted by it?
turns.zh: 是啊。有句话说得好：如果你开始解释，就输了。在这件事上，有很大一部分人始终秉持"母乳喂养才是唯一正确方式"的观念，认为其他选择都是次优方案。我无意去说服他们。但关键在于，要放大那些真正需要我们产品的人的需求——比如使用配方奶粉的83%家庭，确保他们的声音被听到。这确实是品牌建设的深刻启示。如何避免放大那些不该被听见的声音，或被其分散注意力？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting, and I don't know how much you want to talk about this, but I know initially the brand strategy was basically breast is not best. Formula is just as good. And what I'm hearing is you kind of realized you're not going to convince people of that and it's more lean into people that already understand.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我不知道你想多深入探讨这个话题，但我知道最初你们的品牌策略基本上是强调“母乳并非最佳选择”，配方奶粉同样优秀。但我听说你们后来意识到，根本无法说服人们接受这种观点，反而应该专注于那些已经认同这一理念的人。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah. And I think another major belief I have is no brand, and I do fundamentally believe this, no brand should ever be in a position of pointing fingers to something that's better or worse. Our only job, and I wish politics would also do this, our only job is to talk about what we do and why we exist and why we believe our product is good. And I would say the flip is the same in formula. If a mother out there has access to another brand of formula that is more accessible, maybe more affordable, and it suits their baby, then good for them. And I should never be a company in a position pointing to a competitor or another way of feeding saying that it's worse off, ever.
turns.zh: 是的。我另一个坚定的信念是，任何品牌都不应指责其他产品优劣。我们唯一的职责——我真心希望政界也能如此——就是讲述我们自身的价值主张，解释我们存在的意义，以及为何相信自己的产品出色。同样在配方奶粉领域，同样适用。如果有妈妈能获得更易获取、更实惠且适合宝宝的其他品牌产品，那对他们而言再好不过了。我们绝不应以居高临下的姿态贬低竞争对手或其他喂养方式。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my God. This is, I feel, like a secret sauce of just how to get it done half the time. And I really, really do believe the power of branding the mundane is so successful. I mean, we brand, to be fair, I actually feel like that this was a page out of the Airbnb book. Do you remember going back early days when we were doing customer service deep dives? What were the issues that customers were having? And we branded a program called Air Dives. Do you remember Air Dives?
turns.zh: 天哪。我觉得这简直是把事情做成的秘诀，关键在于能事半功倍地把事情搞定。我真的、真的深信，让平凡事物拥有品牌效应的力量非常有效。说真的，公平地讲，我觉得这简直是照搬了Airbnb的模式。还记得早期我们深入研究客户服务时吗？当时客户都遇到了哪些问题？我们还专门打造了一个叫“Air Dives”的项目。你们还记得“Air Dives”吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: And this program just became this thing where everyone wanted to know on a Friday what was the latest Air Dive. And really what an Air Dive was was an analysis of customer service tickets and customer service pain points. But how much better is Air Dive than a customer service analysis? So much better. So I think a lot of learnings on just the power of branding and storytelling your workflows and your frameworks and what it means to do your job, often keeps people motivated, too. And it creates memory recall a lot better, too. So now when you prefer Slack channels, they're all like, I don't even want to name them because I'm going to give you-
turns.zh:
如今，这个项目已然成了每周五大家热议的焦点——大家都想知道最新一期的“空中跳水”（Air Dive）内容。所谓“空中跳水”，其实就是对客户服务工单和痛点的深度分析。但相比于传统的客户服务分析，“空中跳水”又有何过人之处呢？其优势显而易见。因此，我深信，品牌塑造、故事化呈现工作流程与框架，以及明确工作意义等要素，往往能更好地激发团队动力。这种方式还能显著提升信息留存效果。

如今在Slack频道上，大家都争相分享案例——尽管有些名字因涉及保密协议不能透露，但我还是能举几个例子。比如“三叶草计划”（Project Shamrock）、“伐木工计划”（Project Lumberjack）、“Got B 2022”等。这些项目名称背后都蕴含着深刻的含义。以法律合规审批为例，我们需要确保所有内容声明都符合法律要求。为此，我们创建了“神秘购物计划”，监管团队每月开展暗访检查，发现的信息误导或理解偏差由Bobbie团队负责修正。但与被动接受法律报告的会议相比，神秘购物会议更能激发团队主动性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I was going to ask. I'd love some examples and I know they're going to sound ridiculous to an outsider, but what are some examples of things? And you can say like Bobbie Blank, or what's your naming convention?
turns.zh: 别啊，我正想问呢。这些例子听起来肯定很夸张，但能不能举几个具体的例子？比如Bobbie Blank的命名规则之类的。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my God. Project Shamrock. I'm not going to tell you what that's about. Project Lumberjack. Ooh, Got B 2022. I can give you so much insight into what these are and I'll give you an example of it. We have legal approvals that need to get made and these legal approvals on content claims have to happen. And I was like, okay, well how do we make sure everyone sticks to the quality SOP that legal wants set for all of the claims we have to have in place? So we created a program called the Secret Shopping Program, and our regulatory legal team go out and they do their own secret shopping once a month and then they report back on any misleading claims or ones that aren't fully understood that Bobbie needs to go back and update. But having a secret shopping meeting is very different to potentially coming in and listening to legal report out in your claims mishaps.
turns.zh: 天哪！比如“三叶草计划”，我可不能说太多细节。“伐木工计划”。还有“Got B 2022”。我可以详细讲讲这些项目背后的故事。比如法律合规审批，我们需要确保所有内容声明都符合法律要求。于是我们创建了“神秘购物计划”，监管团队每月开展暗访检查，发现的信息误导或理解偏差由Bobbie团队负责修正。但神秘购物会议和被动接受法律报告的会议相比，前者更能激发团队主动性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of legal mishaps and copy nuances, one of my favorite memories of you is I was in San Francisco on Divisadero outside, I think, The Mill, and you were just running by heading somewhere and we started chatting. You were heading, I believe, to the warehouse that you're manufacturing the early versions of Bobbie, and apparently the FDA showed up and shut you down because of some misleading communication in the news, as you're launching. I'd love to hear that story because I love it.
turns.zh: 说到法律纠纷和文案细节，我最难忘的经历是在旧金山Divisadero街上，当时我记得是在The Mill附近。你正要去某个地方，我们就聊了起来。我记得你当时要去仓库检查早期Bobbie产品的生产情况吧。结果FDA因为你们在发布产品时存在误导性信息，勒令停产。这故事太精彩了，我超爱听。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: By the way, how you just transitioned from one example I just gave to that was absolutely exceptional, speaking of content mishaps.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，你从我刚刚举的例子直接过渡到这个故事，转换得太自然了。说到内容失误，这正是你作为播客主持人的过人之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate that.
turns.zh: 真心感谢。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: This is why you're such a good podcast host, Lenny.
turns.zh: 这就是你为什么是位出色的播客主持人，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're so kind.
turns.zh: 你太贴心了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: You're so good.
turns.zh: 你太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you, Laura.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Laura。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Oh, my god, that moment. I do remember bumping into you. I was in an identity crisis. Yeah, early days. I think the one big learning I've had is that when you're in an industry where you are disrupting, I mean truly disrupting the status quo, you're going to be met with some reactions, people, or in our case government agencies who aren't happy about what you're doing. It was early days, we just launched a pilot and the FDA showed up at our warehouse and they didn't like the way that we were labeling the product. We had to pull all of our product from the market, we had to relabel everything and we had to work with the agency for another year before we could bring our products back. For startup world, that was a huge, I wouldn't even say it was a pivot, it was a patient pause, thinking sure that we could get back on track and build intentions with the FDA again.
turns.zh: 天哪，那个时刻。我确实记得和你偶遇过。我当时正经历身份认同危机。是啊，那还是创业初期。我最大的收获是，当你所在的行业正在颠覆现状时，必然会遭遇各种阻力——无论是竞争对手，还是像我们这样不被政府监管部门待见的初创公司。当时刚起步，我们刚推出试点项目，FDA（美国食品药品监督管理局）就突然造访了我们的仓库，他们对我们的产品标签不满。我们不得不将所有产品下架，重新贴标签，还和监管部门耗了一年才让产品重新上市。对创业公司来说，这简直是巨大的挑战。我甚至不愿称之为战略调整，更像是耐心休整，重新与FDA建立信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another example of slowth, maybe.
turns.zh: 或许这就是"慢节奏"的另一种体现。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Another example of slowth, yes.
turns.zh: 没错，又一个"慢节奏"的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you personally stay motivated and keep morale up within the company during that period?
turns.zh: 那段时期，你是如何在公司内部保持积极性和士气的？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Well, I found out I was pregnant with my third child right after.
turns.zh: 嗯，紧接着我发现自己怀了第三个孩子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: There's something about also growing your personal life while professionally it's happening. There's a little bit of give and take as well. So sometimes in moment of professional slowth, you might find that there's personal growth. That's exactly what I found. So I mean, yeah, during this journey I went on from being inspired by my first kid where I wasn't able to breastfeed and then had two more along the journey. And I don't know, I've actually never spoken about this, but I do think there's a beautiful marriage in that personal and professional growth that you can have and you kind of need to find moments where you lean into one and maybe the other. And then there's moments, like I kind of feel like I'm going through right now, where both of them are just on fire and you can't slow them down.
turns.zh: 在事业蒸蒸日上的同时，个人生活也在成长，这其中有得有失。有时职业上的停滞，恰恰能促进个人成长。这正是我经历的。比如，在创业之路上，从最初因无法母乳喂养而倍感挫败，到后来又迎来两个孩子。说实话，我从未公开过这些，但我深知事业与家庭的双重成长需要找到平衡点，适当侧重于其中一方。当然，现在我正经历人生另一个高光时刻——事业与家庭双线火热，根本停不下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It might be a good time to chat about that. So you have this fast-growing business, you have three kids. Your partner is also a founder, also very busy. How do you manage all of these things?
turns.zh: 或许现在正是探讨这个话题的好时机。你的公司发展迅速，又有三个孩子，另一半也是创始人，同样忙碌不堪。你们是如何平衡这一切的？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: That question is actually probably the most common question I get from new founders, those that are aspiring entrepreneurs, on just like how do you do it all? I mean, a lot of it's your infrastructure, it's your... Actually, hold on a second. I'm going to do something I don't think you've done on a podcast before. Hold on. This is my EA. I'm going to pull this woman in. Everyone just needs to say hi to Kendra. This woman.
turns.zh: 这个问题其实是我最常被新创始人或有志创业者问到的：如何兼顾事业与家庭？答案很大程度上取决于你的基础架构和团队协作。等一下，我要做件在播客上从未做过的事。等等。这位是我的行政助理，肯德拉。大家和她打个招呼吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hi, Kendra.
turns.zh: 嗨，肯德拉。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I'm introducing her because the power of a support system to be able to do what you do, I mean, you are an extension, my leverage, my everything. And never leave.
turns.zh: 我要介绍她，是因为一个支持系统能让你成就非凡——我的意思是，她是我的延伸，我的助力，我的全部。永远别离开。

turns.speaker: Kendra
turns.en: I'm not going anywhere.
turns.zh: 我哪儿也不会去。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I'd be so screwed. And everyone should not only know the power and leverage of their person, but the level of appreciation and celebration you need to have for them is just huge.
turns.zh: 那我可就完蛋了。每个人不仅要认识到对方的力量和助力，还要知道对他们的感激与赞美之情是何等深厚。

turns.speaker: Kendra
turns.en: I always feel celebrated, so thank you. I appreciate it.
turns.zh: 我总能感受到被赞美，所以谢谢你。我很感激。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do people find a Kendra of their own? That's the million-dollar question.
turns.zh: 人们如何找到属于自己的肯德拉？这可是个价值百万美元的难题。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Well, first, you don't take this one. This is a poach-free podcast.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，别想挖走她。这可是个禁止挖人的播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Her name Lauren, not-
turns.zh: 她叫劳伦，不叫——

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yes, that's right.
turns.zh: 对，就是这个名字。

turns.speaker: Kendra
turns.en: We should have code names.
turns.zh: 我们应该用代号。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: There's no last names here. How do you find your Kendra? I will say it took multiple interviews and it's all about chemistry. I think it's about chemistry and finding somebody that you genuinely care about. I genuinely care about you, your heart, your kids, your family, and I think finding that connection is really important.
turns.zh: 这里大家都不用姓氏。要怎么找到自己的肯德拉呢？我得说，经历了多次面试，关键在于化学反应。我觉得这关乎化学反应，要找到真正在乎你的人。我真心在乎你、你的心、你的孩子、你的家庭，我认为建立这种联结至关重要。

turns.speaker: Kendra
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Yeah. You know what's also funny, too, I think there's this feeling, and I would hear this from folks, how do you do it all? And I think we also just need to be very transparent. It takes a lot of work to do it all. I, as an operator, am very proud of the infrastructure I have built. I mean, we have calendars on our walls, we have calendars for our kids. We have back and forth birthday planning. It's additional help in the house. My nanny is the other extension in our house. (00:39:10): I mean, I don't know what we would do without Clifford. He is everything for us and I also have to see him as an extension to our parenting. But that is, I think, the only way to get through the chaos and the only way to embrace the all, is you actually need to put in the work to build the infrastructure, the systems, the frameworks, and then every month, or sometimes in our case on a weekly basis, me and my husband, we have a meeting every Sunday and it's walking through the agendas. Who's going to what TaeKwonDo classes this week? Or who's trading off on birthday parties or parent-teacher meetings. Because you're right, a dual CEO-founder household and three kids, it will age you fast if you don't have it.
turns.zh: 是啊。你知道吗，还有件挺有趣的事，我发现很多人都会问：你怎么能做到这一切？我觉得我们只需要保持坦诚。做这一切确实需要付出很多努力。作为一名创业者，我为自己搭建的这套体系深感自豪。比如，我们的墙上挂着日历，孩子们的日历也贴满了墙。生日派对的策划更是需要反复沟通。保姆就是我们家庭的另一位得力助手。（00:39:10）说真的，要是没有克利福德，我们都不知道该怎么办。他对我们来说就是全世界，我也把他视为养育孩子的延伸。但我认为，要想应对生活中的混乱，拥抱全局，关键在于付出努力搭建基础设施、建立体系和框架。每个月——有时我们每周都会和丈夫开周会——我们会逐项过一遍日程安排：这周谁去上跆拳道课？谁轮流筹备生日派对？谁去参加家长会？因为说真的，作为双重CEO创始人家庭，同时还要养育三个孩子，如果没有这样的安排，真的会把人累垮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It also makes me think a little bit about what you talked about earlier where, when things slow down a little bit in the business, there's an opportunity to lean into that part of life and then kind of get ahead on some stuff, in theory.
turns.zh: 这也让我想起你之前提到的，当事业进展稍微放缓时，理论上就有了机会去专注于生活中的其他方面，从而提前完成一些事务。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Totally, totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of the business, I imagine you never started a D2C business before this. Also, you mentioned you've never formulated a baby formula prior to this. Clearly, it's working out. What's a lesson there of just doing something you've never done? Is that something you imagined is a good idea? Maybe looking back, maybe it doesn't matter. What have you learned about just this idea of doing something totally new and different?
turns.zh: 说到事业，我想你之前从未创办过直接面向消费者的品牌。另外，你提到在此之前从未研发过婴儿配方奶粉。显然，现在做得很成功。做从未做过的事，有什么经验教训吗？是预先设想过这是个好主意吗？回头看，或许这无关紧要。但你从零到一做完全新事物，学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I think one of the biggest beliefs is that an ounce of naivety will be your biggest secret to success. And I think the word even naivety sometimes gets a bad rap, but naivety is the definition of creativity and innovation and canvas and white space and opportunity. And I definitely went into starting this company with a level of naivety to how regulated it was, to the stigma associated with it, to how hard it would be. But that has allowed me to continue to look at the status quo differently. (00:41:15): I don't, because I don't fully understand it, and I have applied those same principles even into how I hire people because I do think... I'm now wondering who's going to watch this on my team, because obviously we have some specialists, but this is generalists who make the world go round. I think sometimes putting the most unlikely people who have an ounce of naivety to what it takes to win and succeed are the ones that are going to drive the biggest impact.
turns.zh: 我认为，最重要的信念之一是，一份天真之心将成为你成功的最大秘诀。甚至有时，“天真”这个词会被误解，但天真正是创造力与创新、空白画布与机遇的定义。创办这家公司时，我确实带着对行业监管程度、公众偏见以及挑战之严峻的某种天真。但这种天真让我得以以不同视角审视现状。（00:41:15）：我不这样认为，因为我对它了解不够深入。我甚至将这些原则应用于招聘员工的过程中，因为我坚信……现在我在想，我的团队里谁会观看这个视频？显然我们有一些专业人才，但真正让世界运转的还是那些通才。我认为，有时那些对成功与胜利条件怀有天真之心、看似最不可能胜任的人，反而会创造出最深远的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it makes me think of a couple of things that I'll just share real quick. One is I was listening to an interview with Mr. Beast who is the number one YouTube creator on TikTok. I think he's got the biggest TikTok, and he talked about how he's got this business he's building, which is like a new way of creating content. And anytime he hires someone from a traditional Hollywood movie-making established kind of background, he's like, "They know what they're doing. They're going to help me legitimize this thing, make it scale." He's like, "Every time, they never work out. They just don't see what we're doing here. They don't understand how this is different and they just slow everything down." And he finds just finding really young, hungry, hardworking people that can learn and understand what he's done end up working a lot better.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种观点。由此引发了我的几点思考，简单分享一下。其一，我最近听了YouTube头号创作者Mr. Beast的访谈。他在TikTok上的粉丝数居首。他谈到自己正在打造的业务——一种全新的内容创作模式。每次从传统好莱坞电影制作背景的人才中招聘时，他都会想：“他们经验丰富，能帮我让这项事业合法化，实现规模化。”但结果每次都失败了。因为这些人看不到他的创新之处，总想用老方法拖慢进度。相反，他发现那些年轻、上进、勤奋、愿意学习并理解他所做之事的人，最终能更好地助力业务发展。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Always.
turns.zh: 始终如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other interesting insight is I'm doing a series right now on B2B businesses and how the biggest B2B companies started and so far I'm finding 70% of the founders had no specific background or skill in the area. They went in to say it's security or sales or something like that. So there's a lot of examples of this.
turns.zh: 另一个有趣的发现是，我最近正在做一个关于B2B企业的系列报道，研究大型B2B公司的创始历程。到目前为止，我发现70%的创始人在涉足该领域前并无特定背景或技能。他们只是声称自己懂安全、懂销售之类的。这样的例子比比皆是。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I'll give you one example of someone who's in C who's just an absolute rockstar. Our girl who leads marketing is an Emmy Award news anchor. She's not your traditional marketer. She came in asking me to... She was like, "What does CAC mean? Do we need to look at this LTV number?" And the reason I wanted her in C was because she was the complete antithesis to what we would normally define as a good performance marketer. I wanted someone in C who got media, who got brand and storytelling, and she operates like a news anchor. And in many ways I would look to the team that she's built and think that we maybe have more of a media company than we do a marketing team. And that has been the fuel for the brand that you see today, 100%. And then you hire, unlike the people in those positions and especially senior positions, they're going to do exactly the same throughout the business as well.
turns.zh: 我给你举个例子，C部门里有个绝对的明星人物。我们负责营销的姑娘曾是艾美奖新闻主播。她可不是传统意义上的营销人。她一进来就问我：“CAC（客户获取成本）是什么意思？我们需要关注LTV（客户终身价值）数据吗？”我之所以想让她加入C部门，正是因为她与我们通常定义的优秀绩效营销人截然相反。我需要一个既懂媒体又擅长品牌与故事叙事的人，而她就像个新闻主播。在很多方面，我看着她组建的团队，觉得我们这儿可能更像家媒体公司而非营销团队。这正是成就如今品牌形象的核心驱动力——百分之百如此。然后再来看招聘情况，与那些职位（尤其是高级职位）的人不同，他们在整个公司范围内都会执行完全相同的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. It makes me think of Airbnb a bit. Also, the browser company. We had the founder of that company on here and they have a storytelling team within their company. Their job is tell the story.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这让我想起了Airbnb。还有那家浏览器公司。我们曾邀请过那家公司的创始人来做分享，他们公司内部有一个讲故事的团队。他们的职责就是讲述故事。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you talked about how you're hiring people that aren't necessarily deep in a specific skill that you need them to do. What is it that you look for instead that you think is important for them to figure out what they need to be doing?
turns.zh: 你之前提到，在招聘时，并不一定要求应聘者精通某项特定技能。那你更看重什么？你认为哪些特质对他们理解工作需求很重要？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Curiosity. A lot of curiosity and just openness to what's out there. I definitely look for people who have the ability to make decisions and move fast and not get worried about the outcome. That is the biggest learning in a startup. The secret is momentum and just keeping momentum. And if we try and perfect everything, you just miss the boat. And I believe that, what's the common saying, perfect is the enemy of good, or something.
turns.zh: 好奇心。保持强烈的好奇心，以及对外界事物的开放态度。我特别看重那些能果断决策、行动迅速且不为结果担忧的人。这才是初创公司最重要的学习之道。秘诀在于保持势头和动能。如果我们一味追求完美，就会错失良机。我相信有句话怎么说来着，完美是优秀的敌人，还是怎么说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's the one.
turns.zh: 对，就是这句话。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, it really is. So I look for people who just want to do it, just get it done. Again, part of that is just rolling up your sleeves and not questioning your job. When I find in interviews and people are really questioning the lanes they're going to be in and the job they're going to do, or "I don't do that." That's saying, "I don't do that." A huge flag. You do do it. If you're joining this company, if you're within a certain work stream or a certain department and you're behind what the company's working on, in many ways we need people who do do that. So I look for just optimistic doers.
turns.zh: 确实如此。所以我寻找那些想把事情做成、能把工作完成的人。这其中就包括卷起袖子埋头干活，不质疑自己职责的能力。面试中如果有人对自己未来的职位定位、工作内容存疑，或者说“我不做这个”，那就是个危险信号。他们应该参与进来，融入公司的某个工作流或部门，跟上公司的步伐。我们需要能做到这些的人。所以我寻找乐观的实干家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's such a cool phrase of how to simplify it, what you want to hire and just optimistic doers. There's so many people that have big ideas and pontificate strategy, and you just need people doing the thing.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个说法。把招聘需求简化成“乐观的实干家”真是妙极了。太多人空谈大局、指点战略，而我们真正需要的是能埋头做事的人。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: 100%. I call it intellectual ejaculation, which, if that's not allowed of the podcast, [inaudible 00:45:52] totally wiped.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我把这叫做“智力高潮”，如果播客不允许说这个词，那就当我没说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's allowed. I'll allow it.
turns.zh: 播客允许啊，我可以说。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you're talking about momentum. I want to talk about growth. A lot of this podcast is about growth strategy, how companies grow. You're building a D2C company. D2C is really hard. There's been so many attempts. Most fail, most people can't figure out how to do it scalably. So many challenges. What have you learned about growing D2C company? What's worked well for you?
turns.zh: 好的，你现在谈的是动量问题。我想聊聊增长。这期播客主要讲增长策略，讲公司如何实现增长。你正在打造一家D2C公司。D2C模式确实很难。过去有过很多尝试，大多数都失败了，多数人无法找到可扩展的运营方法，挑战重重。你在D2C公司增长方面有何心得？哪些策略效果显著？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: This narrative of D2C isn't working, or D2C is over, D2C is dead. It kills me. Because we're being way too reductionist in that message. D2C isn't dead. Just the approach for how people did D2C is a bit dated. We should not be paying for every customer and we should be very careful that people aren't getting hooked on the drug that is paid marketing or performance marketing. And I think that drug, and then obviously as we start to see changes on the way certain performance works, it just becomes more expensive and people are resetting how they do performance marketing. The short of it is D2C is not dead. How you drive people to D2C, how you acquire customers, how you build sustainable businesses, that needs to change.
turns.zh: 那种认为D2C模式行不通、已过时、彻底失败的说法真让我头疼。因为我们对这个模式的解读太过简单化了。D2C模式并没有死，只是人们原有的运营方式有些过时了。我们不该为每个客户埋单，也要警惕用户对付费营销或效果营销上瘾。随着效果营销机制发生变革，成本不断攀升，人们也正在重新调整策略。总之，D2C模式并没有过时。关键在于如何引流、获取客户，以及打造可持续的商业模式，这些都需要创新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what is it that you've done that allows you to do that? I imagine a lot of it is word-of-mouth, which everyone always wants. "How do we do more word-of-mouth?" So what's worked? How do you do that?
turns.zh: 那你们做了哪些成功之举呢？我猜很大程度上依赖口碑传播，这是大家梦寐以求的。"如何提升口碑效应？"具体怎么做？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Well, I mean, the three major pieces of it is that the focus on commerce, content and community.
turns.zh: 主要有三个核心要素：专注商业化、内容生态和社区运营。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Commerce, content and community.
turns.zh: 商业化、内容生态和社区运营。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: So commerce, content and community. But most D2C businesses have put commerce at the top of their list. We flipped it. It's now content, community and commerce, and building good content that is really smart SEO, that has the ability to drive people back to your site to be able to build you as a thought leader. That's really hard and it takes a lot of work. As an example, five years ago we started a platform called Milk Drunk, separate to Bobbie. Milk Drunk Blog. And the reason why we started it is because we realize that there was a dearth of education in the world of formula out there. (00:48:15): And what people were really looking for was good recommendations, usability charts, how to make formula, how long does formula last? So we wanted to become the content leaders in that, with the hypothesis, and it's holding true five years later, with the hypothesis that if we win on content and as a thought leader, that will drive back to Bobbie. And today I'm going to give you a totally random example. If you do a cursory Google search for something like "How long does formula last?" Milk Drunk is showing up between the CDC and the bum on the first page of Google? That SEO work and that content building and thought leadership and credibility does take a lot of work. And in the meantime, I've had to squat away requests to put another 100,000, another 300,000 every month into paid marketing because the moment that drug starts, it's very easy to keep it going.
turns.zh: 所以，商业、内容和社区。但大多数D2C企业都把商业放在首位。我们却反其道而行之。现在是内容、社区和商业。打造优质内容实际上就是精明的SEO策略，能吸引人们重返你的网站，树立你作为行业领袖的形象。这非常困难，需要付出大量努力。举个例子，五年前我们创立了与Bobbie独立的平台——Milk Drunk博客。创立它的初衷是意识到市场上缺乏母婴护理知识。（00:48:15）人们真正需要的是优质推荐、实用指南、配方奶粉制作方法、配方奶粉保质期等信息。因此我们决定成为这方面的内容领军者——五年后实践证明了这个假设：只要在内容上胜出并树立行业权威，就能将流量引回Bobbie平台。今天我要给你们举个随机例子。如果你在谷歌上搜索“配方奶粉保质期多长？”相关问题，Milk Drunk会出现在CDC（美国疾病控制与预防中心）和某个博客之间。这说明SEO优化和内容建设、树立权威及建立信任确实需要付出巨大努力。与此同时，我不得不拒绝每月追加10万、30万美元付费营销的请求，因为一旦开始烧钱，就很难停下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think Airbnb is a great example of that. During COVID, they shut down paid growth and I think they've turned it on, but it's a tiny component, which is really unusual and really rare, where you have paid growth, you're sending tons of money, Facebook, and then you stop. It's so hard to stop because growth slows and no one ever wants to do that. And it's interesting, coming back to using a crisis as an opportunity, Airbnb use that as an opportunity to get off that drug.
turns.zh: 我认为Airbnb就是一个很好的例子。疫情期间，Airbnb暂停了付费增长计划，但如今他们又重新启用了这一策略。不过付费增长只占很小的比例，这非常罕见。通常付费增长会投入大量资金，比如Facebook的广告，但一旦停止投入，增长就会放缓，几乎没有公司愿意这么做。有趣的是，Airbnb把危机转化为机遇，成功摆脱了这种增长依赖。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: That's right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you think about the pie chart of what helps Bobbie grow, how much of it would you say is just like make an awesome product that people talk about with other moms and it spreads like that, versus SEO and content and paid?
turns.zh: 如果你看Bobbie增长的因素占比图，你认为其中有多少是靠打造令人惊叹的产品，让妈妈们口口相传，从而实现病毒式传播？又有多少来自SEO、内容和付费营销？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: 60% of it is your product and the package around the product, which is your brand. So even if you did nothing to market your brand, your product and brand is 60% of it. And then the last 40% is how do you get the word out there? How do you ensure the word-of-mouth, mom begets mom? That has to happen. That flywheel will only happen if they're able to look at a product that they fully believe in and a brand that speaks to them. And without that, you're going to be a fast-fashion company, which is also my worst nightmare, the fear that people get distracted by the 40% and the 60% actually is just mediocre.
turns.zh: 60%是你的产品和围绕产品的包装，这构成了你的品牌。所以即便你不做任何品牌营销，你的产品和品牌本身就占据了60%的价值。剩下的40%在于如何让口碑传播开来？如何确保用户会口口相传？这才是关键所在。只有当用户看到他们深信不疑的产品，以及能与他们产生共鸣的品牌时，口碑效应才会产生。若做不到这一点，你最终只会沦为快时尚公司——这简直是我最可怕的噩梦。人们会被那40%和60%的表象所迷惑，而真正的东西却平庸无奇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I wasn't planning to ask, but I thought it'd be interesting and we can cut this if it's not interesting, is Emily Oster, she's one of the, I think, pioneers of breastfeeding is not as great as people say necessarily. Has that been really important to Bobbie in this industry? What do you think of Emily Oster? I'm a huge fan, so I hope you're also a big fan.
turns.zh: 有些话我本不打算问的，但我觉得挺有意思的，如果不感兴趣的话我们可以跳过。她叫艾米丽·奥斯特，我认为她是母乳喂养领域的先驱之一，但人们常说母乳喂养比实际好得多。这对博比来说在这个行业里很重要吗？你们对艾米丽·奥斯特有什么看法？我可是她的超级粉丝，希望你们也能成为她的忠实拥趸。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: We are massive fans of Emily and Emily's a massive fan of Bobbie. She is my idol. She's the one who got me through my first year of pregnancy and then beyond. She has been a really, really important voice. And actually she has kind of set the stage for the power of data to bust myths. I mean, just like you said, she's come out and said, "There is no study, no study at all out there that you can point to that can qualify why breastfeeding is better." And to have an economist, a professor, come out and to be able to underscore that and point to where that is the case and why it is the case. I mean, it's so much better than a company. To be fair, companies are brands coming out trying to say that. So I am acutely aware that, as a business and as a brand, sometimes we need to bring in other credible voices. And my God, Emily is one of those.
turns.zh: 我们都是艾米丽的忠实粉丝，她也是博比的超级粉丝。她是我的偶像。她帮助我度过了怀孕第一年及之后的时光。她一直是一个非常重要的声音。实际上，她为用数据打破迷思奠定了基础。就像你说的，她站出来说：“没有任何研究——任何研究都没有——能证明母乳喂养更好。”让一位经济学家、教授站出来强调这一点，并指出其依据和原因，这比公司的说辞强多了。说实话，公司往往只是打着品牌旗号来宣传。所以我深知，作为一家企业和品牌，有时我们需要引入其他权威声音。天啊，艾米丽就是这样的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Okay, great. I'm glad. I'm glad you love her. I've been reading all our books. I think I just read that section.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，太好了。很高兴你喜欢她。我一直在读我们的书。我想我刚读完那部分内容。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: You read her books. I love it. You're not a dad yet, you'll like all of them, Family Firm.
turns.zh: 你读过她的书。我太高兴了。你还没当爸爸呢，你会喜欢她所有的书的，比如《家庭公司》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, the first two. The first two. Cribsheet. I'll stop there, I think. And I was actually just reading the breastfeeding section and it's funny, one of the only remaining benefits of breastfeeding is less cow farts and creating methane. Unrelated to your child, there's a cow component.
turns.zh: 好的，前两本。前两本。《育儿手册》。我想就到这儿吧。我刚读了母乳喂养那部分内容，很有意思的是，母乳喂养仅存的好处之一就是减少奶牛放屁和产生甲烷。这和你的孩子无关，但涉及奶牛的因素。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: We do want to cut down on the farts.
turns.zh: 我们确实想减少奶牛放屁的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We do. We do. Not what I thought of when I thought of why should I go with formula or not. Maybe just zooming out a little bit and to kind of close, are there any other lessons that you've learned along this journey about building a company, hiring, team building, anything along those lines? Creating urgency, creating momentum?
turns.zh: 确实如此。我们确实想减少奶牛放屁的情况。这不是我当初考虑是否该用配方奶粉时会想到的问题。或许退一步说，在结束前，你们在创业过程中还有哪些其他经验教训？比如招聘、团队建设之类的？比如营造紧迫感、形成发展势头？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, momentum. Momentum really is it. We did this a good bit at Airbnb too. I think as a founder and as a CEO or for any leader out there, your job is not just to keep people going on momentum. Your job is to make momentum. And sometimes that momentum has to be manufactured. And that has been one of my biggest lessons on just how, as leaders and people starting companies, how do you force yourself? And sometimes when it's early on, you're actually just doing it to yourself, creating manufactured deadlines and launch dates. (00:53:36): The amount of times people say to me, "Why are we launching this May 1st?" And I'm like, "Just because we said it. Because if we don't do it now, we may never do it." It was something we were talking about the last day on just how important it is to look at the fuel that keeps you going and how you have to kind of force those milestones to get you there. So yeah, I would say manufacture yourself some momentum.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，动量。动量才是关键。我们在Airbnb也经常这么做。我认为，作为创始人、CEO或任何领导者，你的职责不只是让团队保持前进的势头，更要主动创造动量。有时这种动量必须是人为制造的。这也是我学到的最宝贵的经验之一——作为领导者和创业者，如何逼迫自己前进？尤其在初期阶段，你可能不得不自设截止日期和发布日期。（00:53:36）每次有人问我“为什么我们要在5月1日发布产品？” 我都会回答：“因为我们说定了日期。再不行动，可能就永远做不成了。” 这正是我们在最后一天讨论的重点——审视支撑你前行的燃料，如何通过强制设定里程碑来达成目标。所以我要说，主动为自己制造动量吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I so agree with that. One of my favorite things and one of our former colleagues, Vanessa, taught me this, which is just like, "Let's all set an arbitrary deadline right now." And just make it clear, this is just arbitrary, but it's useful.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同这一点。我的好友、前同事瓦妮莎教会了我一个方法，就是“现在就设定一个随意的截止日期”。要明确说明，这个期限只是随意设定的，但它确实有用。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: It's so true.
turns.zh: 这太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, Laura, we've reached our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 好的，劳拉，接下来我们要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Who?
turns.zh: 谁？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if I told you this was coming, but it is. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready for exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我不知道有没有跟你提过这个环节，但现在要开始了。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好迎接精彩的闪电问答了吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I think I am. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 我想我准备好了。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: One recently, Great by Choice, the author of From Good to Great, amazing.
turns.zh: 最近读的《选择的悖论》（Great by Choice），作者是《从优秀到卓越》（From Good to Great）的作者，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jim Collins?
turns.zh: 吉姆·柯林斯（Jim Collins）？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Some really, really good frameworks. Yes, that's right. Really good frameworks in there. Metabolical, very specific into the world of health, healthcare. Actually, very specifically the takeaway of Metabolical is we don't have a healthcare crisis in this country, we have a health crisis. And it really makes you think about the source, food and how we live our lives. It's amazing. And then I think you a really good traditional one, going back to just brand and for people who are really just looking for a good foundation, I love Purple Cow.
turns.zh: 里面有一些非常非常好的框架。没错，就是这样。里面有很多很棒的框架。比如《新陈代谢》（Metabolical），专门讲健康和医疗领域的，特别是健康危机的问题。它真的让你反思根源——食物和生活方式。太棒了。还有一本传统好书，《紫牛》（Purple Cow），对于那些只想打牢基础的人来说，是个很好的选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I think I have it in my back around here.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这本书。我好像把它落在这附近了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: You do?
turns.zh: 你有？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There it is, yeah. Tiny little book. It's so cute.
turns.zh: 在那儿，太小了。真可爱。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: That is so good.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Also, we could mention Emily Oster's book, Laura, Expecting Better.
turns.zh: 劳拉，我们应该提到艾米丽·奥斯特（Emily Oster）的《期待更好的生活》（Expecting Better）。这本书很经典。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, we should. Expecting Better is a good classic.
turns.zh: 是啊。我们应该提到的。《期待更好的生活》是本经典之作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your list is reminding me of a new book by Peter Attia, that I don't know if you've seen, called Outlive, I think it's called. It's about longevity and how to live longer and all the latest sciences and how to live a longer life. But anyway, that's my answer and I'm asking you questions, so let's move on to the next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 你的书单让我想起彼得·阿蒂亚（Peter Attia）的新书，叫《活得更久》（Outlive）。我不知道你看过没。是关于长寿的，如何活得更久，所有最新的科学研究，以及如何延长寿命的。不过先不说这个，我的问题来了。最近看的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Bad Sisters. Do you have bad sisters?
turns.zh: 《坏姐妹们》（Bad Sisters）。你有坏姐妹吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: About a group of Irish sisters getting up to trouble. Highly recommended.
turns.zh: 讲一群爱尔兰姐妹调皮捣蛋的故事。强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask when you're hiring people?
turns.zh: 太棒了。招聘时你最喜欢问的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Teach me something. Actually, we just talked about that today. Teach me something. Yeah. I love getting someone to, not related to work, not related to their job, something in your life, something you find interesting, just teach me about it.
turns.zh: 教我点东西。实际上，我们今天刚聊过这个。教我点东西。是啊。我喜欢让应聘者讲讲和工作无关、和职位无关的生活中的趣事，让他们教我点东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is it that you look for in their answer that gives you a sense that they're someone that you want to hire?
turns.zh: 从他们的回答中，你能看出哪些特质让你觉得他们是值得录用的人？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Creative, but also just their ability to explain something, and it is a huge indicator. I mean, I'll never forget one guy teaching me how to cook the perfect steak, and now every time I cook a steak, I go back to the way he described it, to someone being able to teach me the foundation of Latin. But if someone's unable to take one thing that they find is core to who they are and what they've done or what they understand and their inability to explain that to you, they may struggle.
turns.zh: 他们既富有创造力，又善于把事情解释清楚，这是一个很重要的指标。我永远忘不了有个人教我如何烹饪出完美牛排，现在每次我做牛排时，都会回想起他当时的描述。还有人能教我拉丁语的基础知识。但如果一个人无法将自己认同的、所做之事或所知晓的核心内容传达给别人，那他们可能会遇到困难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to learn how to cook a perfect steak. I'm going to have to interview you at some point and ask you about that. What's a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love? And especially if it's a baby product, that'll be bonus.
turns.zh: 我想学习如何烹饪完美牛排。我迟早得采访你，问问你这个问题。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？特别是如果是婴儿用品，那就再好不过了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: I mean, yeah, I think Frida Baby's amazing, the nose sucker.
turns.zh: 我是说，没错，我觉得Frida Baby很棒，那个吸鼻器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. The nose sucker.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。吸鼻器。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Actually, no. Sorry, the nose sucker. That's terrible. It's the snot sucker.
turns.zh: 实际上，不对。抱歉，应该是“吸鼻器”。这太糟糕了。应该是“吸鼻涕器”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: As a new parent, you really, really need this, Lenny. Your poor little boy is going to get blocked up and you're going to want to get out that sucker and suck on it-
turns.zh: 作为新手父母，你真的、真的需要这个，莱尼。你可怜的小男孩鼻塞了，而你肯定想拿出那个吸鼻器吸一吸——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, dear.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: ... and get it out. I can see you quickly looking for the next question. Move away from the snot sucker.
turns.zh: ……然后把它拿出来。能看出来你急着想换下一个问题。别再纠结吸鼻器了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, this is great.
turns.zh: 不，这很棒。

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: So I'll leave you with that.
turns.zh: 那就先这样吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. We'll just call the episode The Snot Sucker. So many options. Okay, next question. What's something relatively minor that you've changed in the way that you build/ship product that was minor but had a tremendous impact on your team's ability to execute and ship?
turns.zh: 完美。我们就把这一集叫做《吸鼻器》吧。选项太多了。好的，下一个问题。你在产品开发/交付过程中，改变过哪些相对微小但对团队执行和交付能力影响巨大的做法？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: More recently, async work. Moving away from meeting culture and being able to be in a position where we can work async, whether it's one-hour sprint over Slack, make decisions and go back and forth, 20 people, and then everyone's made a decision by the end of the hour and we're moving forward.
turns.zh: 最近是异步工作。摆脱会议文化，让团队能够异步协作，无论是在Slack上进行一小时的快速决策，20个人参与讨论，最终在一小时内达成共识，然后继续推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a tool that helps you do that or is it just in Slack? "Here's the question we're trying to answer," and everyone-
turns.zh: 有没有工具能帮助实现这一点？还是只在Slack里操作？“这是我们要解决的问题”，然后每个人——

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: You know what? Every so often we try and introduce tools and then it's like we've over-processed this entire thing, when what we really just need to do is all just get our head into the moment we're in and brand it and get it done. So even though I think we've introduced some tools, I know we use some video ones as well. I'm a little bit removed sometimes from everyone working through these tools, but I'm in the Slack world the most.
turns.zh: 你知道吗？我们偶尔会引入一些工具，结果却让整个事情过度流程化，而我们真正需要做的，就是专注于当下，明确目标，完成任务。所以尽管我觉得我们引入了一些工具，比如视频会议工具，我有时也会和团队疏远，但我大部分时间都在Slack世界里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, what is your best advice for a soon-to-be parent, aka, me?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，对即将为人父母的人，也就是我，你有什么最好的建议？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Hire a sitter who you love that you want to have on board every Thursday night and keep your date night with Michelle, whatever your date night is, and just don't worry about the price because the date is worth it, but just lock it in and do it.
turns.zh: 雇一个你喜欢、每周四晚上都能到场的保姆，继续和米歇尔保持约会之夜的传统，无论你们的约会之夜是什么样的，别担心费用，因为这段时光值得珍惜，只要坚持下去就行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We actually have a date night currently with another couple who has two kids, and so we could just maintain that. How early do you hire a sitter to do that, in their age?
turns.zh: 实际上，我们现在和另一对有两个孩子的夫妇一起度过约会之夜，这样做也挺不错的。那么在他们这个年龄段，要多早开始雇保姆呢？

turns.speaker: Laura Modi
turns.en: Second week.
turns.zh: 第二周。
